questions.q: In the following series of reactions identify the major products A and B respectively (bromobenzene -> SO3/H2SO4 -> A -> Br2/Fe -> B).
questions.explain: Do it in two steps. Br is deactivating but directs ortho/para, because its lone pair helps the arenium ion at those positions. Sulfonation goes para, since ortho is more crowded, so A is p-bromobenzenesulfonic acid. For the second step, Br wants the new group ortho/para to itself and SO3H (-M) wants it meta to itself. Positions ortho to Br are also meta to SO3H, so both agree. So B has the new Br next to the old Br, and meta to SO3H.

questions.q: Given below are two statements: Statement I: Nitration of benzene involves the following step (see image). Statement II: Use of Lewis base promotes the electrophilic substitution of benzene. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer.
options: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
questions.explain: Statement I is the real nitration step: H2SO4 protonates HNO3, and the protonated form loses water to give NO2+, the electrophile. So I is correct. Substitution needs a stronger electrophile, and the helpers for that are Lewis acids, which accept an electron pair. A Lewis base would donate pairs and only use up the electrophile. So Statement II is incorrect.

questions.q: Which of the following compound will most easily be attacked by an electrophile?
questions.explain: An electrophile attacks the ring with the most electron density. In phenol, OH donates its lone pair by +M, so it is the strongest activator here. Toluene is activated only weakly by CH3 (+I and hyperconjugation), and benzene is the plain reference. Chlorobenzene is deactivated, because Cl's -I effect outweighs its +M effect. So phenol is attacked most easily.

questions.q: Identify A and B in the following reaction sequence.
questions.explain: Look at what the nitro groups do for the second step. Here A is the trinitro compound with NO2 at both ortho positions and the para position relative to Br. Those NO2 groups pull electrons strongly (-M) from exactly the carbon holding Br, so it becomes electron poor. NaOH is a nucleophile and replaces Br by OH (nucleophilic aromatic substitution). HCl then protonates the phenoxide, so B is 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid). The other options do not have NO2 groups ortho and para to Br, so this substitution would not work.

questions.q: The arenium ion which is not involved in the bromination of aniline is:
questions.explain: The arenium ion is the carbocation intermediate in electrophilic substitution. NH2 donates its lone pair by +M, and that pushes positive charge onto the ortho and para carbons. When the electrophile attacks ortho or para, the charge can land on the carbon carrying NH2 and N can stabilise it (the NH2+ forms). When it attacks meta, the charge never lands on that carbon, so NH2 cannot help. So aniline avoids meta attack, and the meta arenium ion is the one not involved in the reaction.

questions.q: The correct order of reactivity in electrophilic substitution reaction of the following compounds is: A = benzene, B = toluene, C = chlorobenzene, D = nitrobenzene
questions.explain: Reactivity follows electron density in the ring. Toluene is the fastest because CH3 donates by +I and hyperconjugation. Benzene comes next as the reference. Chlorobenzene is slower because Cl pulls electrons by -I more than it gives by +M (it still directs ortho/para, but it slows the reaction). Nitrobenzene is the slowest, as NO2 withdraws by -M and -I. So B > A > C > D.

questions.q: Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of rate of aromatic electrophilic substitution reaction.
questions.explain: Rate of electrophilic substitution goes up with ring electron density, so ask what each compound has on the ring. (c) has a C=O attached to the ring, which pulls electrons (-M), so it is the slowest. (a) has only alkyl groups, which push electrons slightly, and its OH sits on an aliphatic carbon, so it does nothing to the ring. (b) has an OH directly on the ring, which donates by +M. (d) has both an OH and a ring-attached ether O, two +M donors, so it is the fastest. So c < a < b < d.

questions.q: Halogenation of which one of the following will yield m-substituted product with respect to methyl group as a major product?
questions.explain: We want the incoming group meta to CH3. CH3 alone would send it ortho/para to itself, so another group has to be stronger and override it. In o-cresol, OH is the stronger activator (+M), so the electrophile goes ortho/para to OH. The position para to OH is meta to CH3, which gives the answer. In the other options there is no strong activator to overrule CH3, so CH3 still steers the incoming group ortho/para.

questions.q: Arrange the following in increasing order of reactivity towards nitration: A. p-xylene, B. bromobenzene, C. mesitylene, D. nitrobenzene, E. benzene
questions.explain: Nitration is faster when the ring is richer in electrons. Nitrobenzene is the slowest, since NO2 withdraws by -M and -I. Bromobenzene is next: Br is deactivating (-I beats +M) even though it directs ortho/para. Benzene is the reference. p-Xylene is faster because it has two CH3 groups pushing electrons (+I, hyperconjugation), and mesitylene is fastest with three. So D < B < E < A < C.

questions.q: The intermediate X, in the following reaction (phenol + CHCl3/aq. NaOH, then NaOH, H+, giving salicylaldehyde) is:
questions.explain: This is the Reimer-Tiemann reaction. In aqueous NaOH, phenol is converted to phenoxide, which is much more electron rich than phenol. CHCl3 and base make dichlorocarbene, :CCl2, the electrophile. The ortho carbon of the phenoxide attacks it and the ring ends up with CHCl2 at the ortho position. Because the medium is basic, the oxygen stays as O-Na+. Then NaOH hydrolyses CHCl2 to CHO and acid restores OH. So X is the sodium phenoxide with an ortho CHCl2 group.

questions.q: The increasing order of the reactivity of the following compounds towards electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions is: I. chlorobenzene, II. toluene, III. acetophenone
questions.explain: Rate goes with electron density in the ring. Acetophenone (III) has a C=O attached to the ring, which pulls electrons by -M, so it is the slowest. Chlorobenzene (I) is deactivated, since Cl's -I effect beats its +M effect. Toluene (II) is activated by CH3 (+I and hyperconjugation), so it is the fastest. So III < I < II.

questions.q: In Friedel-Crafts alkylation of aniline, one gets:
options: alkylated product with ortho and para substitution
positively charged nitrogen at benzene ring
questions.explain: Aniline has an NH2 group with a lone pair, which makes it a base. AlCl3, the Friedel-Crafts catalyst, is a Lewis acid. So the catalyst reacts with the nitrogen first and forms a salt-like complex, leaving N with a positive charge. That positive N pulls electrons from the ring strongly (-I), so the ring is deactivated and alkylation cannot happen. So the answer is a positively charged nitrogen at the benzene ring.

questions.q: Assertion A: Aniline on nitration yields ortho, meta & para nitro derivatives of aniline. Reason R: Nitrating mixture is a strong acidic mixture.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explain: The nitrating mixture is very acidic, so most aniline is protonated to anilinium (NH3+). NH3+ has no lone pair left and pulls electrons by -I, so it is a meta director. Some free aniline still remains in equilibrium and directs ortho/para. So you get ortho, meta and para products. A is true, R is true, and R explains why the meta product appears.

questions.q: Which of the following compounds will not undergo Friedel Crafts reaction with benzene?
questions.explain: Friedel-Crafts needs the halide to lose Cl and form a carbocation. In vinyl chloride the Cl lone pair delocalises into the C=C, so the C-Cl bond gets partial double-bond character and is stronger and shorter. AlCl3 cannot pull Cl off easily, and the vinyl cation would be very unstable anyway. So vinyl chloride does not undergo the reaction. Allyl chloride gives a resonance-stabilised cation, and the two acid chlorides give acylium ions, so they all work.

questions.q: p-Hydroxybenzophenone upon reaction with bromine in carbon tetrachloride gives:
questions.explain: First decide which ring reacts. One ring has OH (+M, a strong activator), and both rings have the C=O (-M, deactivating). Br2 in CCl4 is mild with no catalyst, so only the OH ring is reactive enough. OH directs ortho/para. Para to OH is already taken by the C=O, so Br goes ortho to OH, which is also meta to the C=O, so both groups agree. The other options put Br on the deactivated ring or in a spot that does not match these directing effects.

questions.q: Consider the given reaction, the Product A is: (aryl alkyl ketone + Br2, AlBr3 in ether)
questions.explain: The C=O group on the ring withdraws electrons by -M, so it deactivates the ring and directs meta. Br2/AlBr3 is the electrophilic ring bromination condition, since the Lewis acid makes Br a strong electrophile. So Br enters the ring meta to the carbonyl group. Bromination on the side chain needs radical or acid conditions, not AlBr3, and ortho/para bromination is not favoured by a meta director. So the answer is the meta-bromo ketone.

questions.q: The major product formed in the Friedel-Craft acylation of chlorobenzene is:
questions.explain: The electrophile is the acylium ion (CH3CO+). Cl is deactivating, because its -I effect beats its +M effect, but its lone pairs still direct the attack ortho/para. Between ortho and para, para wins because it avoids crowding next to Cl. Acylation also stops after one group, because the product is deactivated by C=O. So the major product is 4-chloroacetophenone, p-acetyl chlorobenzene.
